sections.heading: 3.1 NOBLE Architecture
sections.text: Given a standard linear layer f ⁡ ( x ) = x ​ W + b f(x)=xW+b with W ∈ ℝ d in × d out W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}\times d_{\text{out}}} , NOBLE augments it with a low-rank nonlinear branch: f NOBLE ​ ( x ) = x ​ W + b + σ ⁡ ( x ​ W down ) ​ W up f_{\text{NOBLE}}(x)=xW+b+\sigma(xW_{\text{down}})W_{\text{up}} (1) where W down ∈ ℝ d in × r W_{\text{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}\times r} , W up ∈ ℝ r × d out W_{\text{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{out}}} , r ≪ min ⁡ ( d in , d out ) r\ll\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}}) is the bottleneck rank, and σ \sigma is a nonlinear activation function. We evaluated several choices for σ \sigma and find that cosine-based activations perform best (see Section 4 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 CosNet: Recommended Nonlinearity
sections.text: Among several activation functions we evaluate (see Section 4 ), we recommend CosNet , a two-layer cosine nonlinearity operating in the bottleneck space: σ cos ​ ( h ) = cos ⁡ ( ω 2 ⊙ ( M ⋅ cos ⁡ ( ω 1 ⊙ h + ϕ 1 ) ) + ϕ 2 ) \sigma_{\text{cos}}(h)=\cos(\omega_{2}\odot(M\cdot\cos(\omega_{1}\odot h+\phi_{1}))+\phi_{2}) (2) where h ∈ ℝ r h\in\mathbb{R}^{r} is the bottleneck representation, M ∈ ℝ r × r M\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} is a learned mixing matrix, and each dimension i i has learnable frequency ω i \omega_{i} and phase ϕ i \phi_{i} parameters. The cosine activation cos ⁡ ( ω ⊙ x + ϕ ) \cos(\omega\odot x+\phi) has several properties we theorize may be desirable: • Bounded output : Unlike ReLU or GELU, cosine outputs are bounded in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , providing natural regularization. • Smooth and periodic : Enables modeling of periodic patterns and smooth interpolations. • Learnable frequency : The frequency parameters ω \omega control the sensitivity to input variations, adapting to the data distribution. • Learnable phase : The phase parameters ϕ \phi allow shifting the nonlinearity’s operating point.

sections.heading: Learning Rate Scaling.
sections.text: The low-rank structure necessitates careful learning rate treatment. Roughly following μ \mu P ( Yang et al., 2022 ) , we apply elevated learning rates to W up W_{\text{up}} and the CosNet mixing matrix M M , while W down W_{\text{down}} uses the base learning rate. Specifically: lr W up \displaystyle\text{lr}_{W_{\text{up}}} = lr base ⋅ ( min ⁡ ( d in , d out ) r ) 2 ​ γ \displaystyle=\text{lr}_{\text{base}}\cdot\left(\frac{\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})}{r}\right)^{2\gamma} (3) lr M \displaystyle\text{lr}_{M} = lr base ⋅ ( min ⁡ ( d in , d out ) r ) γ M \displaystyle=\text{lr}_{\text{base}}\cdot\left(\frac{\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})}{r}\right)^{\gamma_{M}} (4) where γ = 0.3 \gamma=0.3 is the base learning rate multiplier power (so W up W_{\text{up}} uses exponent 2 ​ γ = 0.6 2\gamma=0.6 ), and γ M = 0.45 \gamma_{M}=0.45 for the mixing matrix.

sections.heading: 3.4 Computational Overhead
sections.text: For typical settings ( d in = d out = d d_{\text{in}}=d_{\text{out}}=d , r = 64 r=64 – 128 128 ), NOBLE adds: • Parameters : 4–12% additional (low-rank matrices + CosNet parameters) • Step time : 7–12% longer (measured on H100 GPUs using with bf16 mixed precision, torch.compile using reduce-overhead mode and fullgraph=True) These percentages are relative to model size : the same rank on a larger model yields proportionally smaller overhead. For example, rank 64 adds 5.7% parameters to our 250M base model but only 4.0% to our 1.5B large model (see Table 1 ). Critically, despite this per-step overhead, the 21–32% reduction in training steps yields net wallclock speedups of 1.17–1.22 × \times .

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Autoregressive LLM Pretraining
sections.text: Setup. We train LLM transformers on OpenWebText ( Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) . The architecture uses GeGLU feedforward blocks ( Shazeer, 2020 ) with hidden dimension 8 3 ​ d \frac{8}{3}d (aligned to 64), RoPE positional encodings ( Su et al., 2024 ) , and RMSNorm ( Zhang and Sennrich, 2019 ) . We test two configurations: • Base : depth 12, width 1024, 8 attention heads, batch 64, lr 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , 250k steps • Large : depth 24, width 2048, 16 attention heads, batch 128, lr 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} , 200k steps Both use weight decay 0.01, β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.98 \beta_{2}=0.98 , sequence length 1024. NOBLE is applied to all linear projections (Q, K, V, output projection, and both FFN layers, we leave ablations on selecting which layers to apply NOBLE to for future work). We ablate across ranks 64, 128, and 256. Results. Table 1 shows that NOBLE consistently achieves lower final loss than the baseline. We report step speedup (ratio of baseline steps to steps needed to reach baseline’s final loss) and wallclock speedup (accounting for per-step overhead). Figure 3 shows the training curves. sections.heading: 4.2.1 ViT-S ImageNet Classification
sections.text: Setup. We train ViT-Small (22M parameters) on ImageNet-1k for 90 epochs with batch size 1024, image size 224, RandAugment, learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.98 \beta_{2}=0.98 , weight decay 0.05, and cosine annealing with 5 warmup epochs. We compare configurations with and without Mixup/CutMix augmentation. Results. Table 3 and Figure 4 reveal an interesting interaction between NOBLE and augmentation. With standard Mixup/CutMix augmentation, NOBLE provides a modest improvement (1.6% lower train loss). However, without Mixup/CutMix, NOBLE’s benefit is more pronounced (5.0% lower train loss) , suggesting that the aggressive label smoothing from these augmentations partially interferes with NOBLE’s fitting capabilities. sections.heading: 4.2.2 Autoregressive Image Token Modeling
sections.text: Setup. We train an autoregressive transformer on discrete image tokens, analogous to LLM training on text tokens. Images are first encoded into discrete tokens using a pretrained VQGAN ( Esser et al., 2021 ) , then we train a causal transformer to predict tokens autoregressively (next-token prediction): • Architecture: depth 12, width 1024, 8 heads (identical to base LLM) • Tokenizer: amused-512 VQGAN with 8192 codebook, 1024 tokens per 512 × \times 512 image (32 × \times 32 grid) • Positional encoding: 2D RoPE (analogous to 1D RoPE for text) • Attention: Causal (raster-scan token order) • Training: batch 64, lr 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.98 \beta_{2}=0.98 , weight decay 0.01, 250k steps • Regularization: None (no dropout, no augmentation) • Class conditioning: Prepended class embedding Results. Table 4 shows that NOBLE improves autoregressive image token modeling, achieving lower eval loss than baseline. This setup is structurally identical to LLM pretraining (next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss), differing only in the token vocabulary (discrete image codes vs. text BPE tokens). Combined with our ViT results (which show improvement when Mixup/CutMix is disabled), this demonstrates that NOBLE benefits both language and image token prediction when aggressive augmentation is not used. sections.heading: Function Smoothness and Regularization
sections.text: To understand NOBLE’s interaction with augmentation, it helps to formalize what smoothness means for a learned function. A function f f is L L -Lipschitz if ‖ f ⁡ ( x ) − f ⁡ ( y ) ‖ ≤ L ​ ‖ x − y ‖ \|f(x)-f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\| for all x , y x,y , bounding how rapidly outputs can change with respect to inputs. The related notion of L L -smooth gradients requires ‖ ∇ f ​ ( x ) − ∇ f ​ ( y ) ‖ ≤ L ​ ‖ x − y ‖ \|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\| ( Nesterov, 2004 ) , bounding the rate of change of the gradient itself, i.e., constraining curvature. A function with a small gradient Lipschitz constant cannot exhibit sharp bends or rapid directional changes. In the frequency domain, this corresponds to energy concentrated in low-frequency Fourier components, while high-frequency components encode rapid oscillations, sharp transitions, and fine-grained local structure ( Rahaman et al., 2019 ) . Many standard regularization techniques implicitly or explicitly encourage such smoothness. Weight decay penalizes large weights, limiting each layer’s Lipschitz constant and thus the composed function’s capacity for rapid variation. Dropout averages over an implicit ensemble of sub-networks, producing predictions smoother than any individual member. Label smoothing ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) softens targets, discouraging sharp decision boundaries. Spectral normalization ( Miyato et al., 2018 ) directly bounds layer-wise Lipschitz constants. Gaussian noise injection is equivalent to Tikhonov regularization ( Bishop, 1995 ; Seghouane et al., 2004 ) , explicitly penalizing high-frequency components ( Camuto et al., 2020 ) . Mixup ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and CutMix enforce that the network interpolates linearly between training points, imposing a direct smoothness constraint. These techniques are effective in part because neural networks exhibit a spectral bias : they naturally learn low-frequency components first and fit high-frequency details only later in training, if at all ( Rahaman et al., 2019 ) . Smoothness regularization amplifies this inductive bias to improve generalization.

sections.heading: Computational Tradeoffs
sections.text: At rank 64–128, NOBLE adds 4–12% parameters and 7–12% step time overhead, but provides 1.26–1.35 × \times step speedup, yielding 1.17–1.21 × \times net wallclock speedup. This represents a favorable tradeoff: practitioners can reach target performance significantly faster despite the per-step cost.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: • Inference overhead : Unlike adapter methods that can be merged post-training, NOBLE adds permanent inference cost (6–12% FLOPs). This may be undesirable for inference-constrained deployments. • Augmentation interaction : We identify that Mixup/CutMix interferes with NOBLE, but do not fully characterize which augmentation strategies are compatible. • Limited vision coverage : We test only ViT classification and autoregressive image token modeling. Other vision tasks (detection, segmentation) might behave differently. • Scale : Our largest model is 1.5B parameters. The observed effects might change at larger scales. • Tokenizer dependence : Our image token results depend on the specific VQGAN tokenizer (amused-512). Other visual tokenizers might yield different results.
